text: Woolly mammoths were hairy elephants of the [[@ice-ages|Ice Age]]. They lived on cold, dry [[@grasslands|grasslands]] across Europe, Asia and North America. When the Ice Age ended, about 10,000 years ago, those grasslands shrank as forests and wetter ground spread.

At the same time, people were hunting them. Most scientists think the two together, a warming [[climate|climate]] and hunting, pushed mammoths to [[extinct|extinction]]. Which mattered more is still argued over.

sec.t:
A woolly mammoth stood about 3 metres tall at the shoulder, roughly as tall as a single-decker bus. It had a coat of long, shaggy hair over a thick, woolly underlayer, and a layer of fat under its skin.

Its ears were small and its tail was short. Both helped, because less skin sticking out means less heat lost. Its long curved tusks may have been used to sweep snow off plants, as well as for fighting and showing off. Some tusks grew more than 4 metres long.

Mammoths ate grasses, herbs and low shrubs. During the cold, dry Ice Age, a huge grassland called the mammoth steppe stretched from Spain to Canada. As the planet warmed, more rain and snow fell, and much of that grassland turned into forest, bog and wet [[@tundra|tundra]]. There was simply less good food.

Climate alone may not explain it, though. Mammoths had survived earlier warm spells. This time, there was something new: people.

Stone Age people hunted mammoths and used every part. In what is now Ukraine, people built [[@cave-to-houses|round huts]] from hundreds of mammoth bones about 15,000 years ago. In North America, stone spear points have been found among mammoth bones.

Mammoths had only one calf every few years, so even a little hunting could hurt a herd that was already short of food. Many scientists think the pressure from [[@stone-age|Stone Age]] hunters, added to a changing climate, was too much.

sec.h: How do we know so much?
sec.t:
Mammoths have been found frozen in the ground in Siberia, sometimes with hair, skin and even food in their stomachs. In 2007, a reindeer herder found a baby mammoth in Russia's Yamal Peninsula, so well kept that scientists could study her trunk and eyelashes. She was named Lyuba.

Tusks hold clues too. A tusk grew in thin layers, a little each day, like the rings of a tree. In 2021, scientists studied the chemistry of those layers in one Alaskan mammoth's tusk. It showed that during its life, the mammoth walked a distance that would nearly circle the Earth twice.

Scientists have also read mammoth [[@dna|DNA]]. It shows they were most closely related to [[@elephants-talk|Asian elephants]], like the ones in India's forests today.

Some scientists want to use DNA to make elephants with mammoth features, such as thick hair and extra fat. Others ask whether it is wise, or kind to the elephants involved. For now, the mammoth is gone, and its relatives in India and Africa face troubles of their own.

text: A forest fire needs three things: fuel, oxygen and heat. Forests are full of fuel, from dry leaves and grass on the ground to dead branches and resin-rich pines. Air supplies the oxygen. All that is needed is a spark.

Sometimes nature provides it, usually with [[@lightning|lightning]]. Far more often, people do: an unattended campfire, burning crop waste, a cigarette, a spark from a machine or a fallen power line. Once a fire starts, hot, dry and windy weather decides how fast it spreads. Long [[@droughts|droughts]] and [[@heatwaves|heatwaves]], which are becoming more common as the planet warms, make forests easier to burn.

st.prompt: In the USA, what starts most wildfires?
st.reveal: Lightning starts a share of wildfires, especially in remote areas, but about 85% are caused by people. Sunshine alone almost never sets a forest alight, though it dries the fuel that makes fires spread.

myth: All forest fires are disasters that should be put out immediately.

Many forests evolved with fire. Small, regular fires clear dead wood and help some seeds sprout. Putting out every fire for decades can let fuel pile up, making later fires bigger and harder to control.

sec.t:
Most forest fires begin on the ground, burning grass, needles and fallen leaves. These ground fires can move slowly and leave big trees scarred but alive. If flames climb up shrubs and low branches into the treetops, they become crown fires. Crown fires race through the [[canopy|canopy]] and can leap across roads and rivers.

Wind is a fire's best friend. It pushes flames forward, brings fresh oxygen and carries glowing embers, sometimes more than a kilometre ahead, starting new spot fires. Fires also run uphill faster, because the flames lean towards the slope and preheat the fuel above. A big fire can create its own wind and even its own thunderclouds.

California, Oregon and other western US states have long, dry summers and forests full of fuel. Strong autumn winds can turn a small fire into a fast-moving disaster. More people now live at the edge of forests, so more homes are in the way. In 2018 the Camp Fire destroyed the town of Paradise, California, and killed 85 people, one of the deadliest US wildfires in a century.

For decades, the US Forest Service tried to stop every fire. Its mascot, Smokey Bear, first appeared in 1944 with the message that only you can prevent forest fires. Preventing careless fires was a good idea. But stopping natural fires too let dead wood build up.

Some [[ecosystem|ecosystems]] depend on burning. Lodgepole pines in Yellowstone National Park have cones sealed with resin that open in the heat of a fire, scattering seeds onto the freshly cleared ground. After huge fires burned about a third of Yellowstone in 1988, young pines sprang up in their millions.

[[indigenous|Indigenous]] peoples in Australia, North America and parts of India have long set small, careful fires to clear undergrowth and keep larger fires away. Many forest managers now use similar planned burns, lit in cool, damp weather, to reduce fuel.

Scientists find that hotter, drier conditions linked to [[@climate-change|climate change]] are making fire seasons longer in many places. Australia's 2019–20 bushfires burned more than 17 million hectares, an area about half the size of Rajasthan, and killed or displaced vast numbers of animals. Smoke from Canadian wildfires in 2023 turned the sky orange over New York City, more than 1,000 km away, and added to [[@air-pollution|air pollution]] for millions of people.

text: If all mosquitoes disappeared, the biggest change would be for people. Mosquitoes spread malaria, dengue, chikungunya, Zika and yellow fever. Malaria alone caused about 282 million cases and 6,10,000 deaths in 2024, according to the World Health Organization. Most of those who died were young children in Africa. A world without mosquitoes would save hundreds of thousands of lives every year.

For nature, the answer is less clear. Mosquitoes are food for fish, frogs, birds, bats and spiders. Some scientists think other insects would quickly fill the gap. Others worry that a few [[foodchain|food chains]], especially in the Arctic and in [[wetland|wetlands]], would be badly shaken. Nobody knows for sure.

st.reveal: Mosquito larvae are a snack for many water animals, from small fish such as guppies to dragonfly nymphs. Some fish are even released into ponds to eat them and control mosquitoes.

n.certNote: Scientists agree that removing disease-carrying mosquitoes would save hundreds of thousands of lives a year. They disagree about what removing all mosquitoes would do to nature, because mosquitoes are food for many animals and help pollinate some plants. Nobody has tested it on a large scale.

sec.t:
Sharks, snakes and tigers get all the scary headlines. But mosquitoes are linked to far more human deaths than any other animal, because of the diseases they carry.

A female mosquito bites to get blood, which she needs to make her eggs. If she has already bitten someone with malaria, tiny [[parasite|parasites]] may travel from her [[saliva|saliva]] into the next person's blood. Dengue and Zika viruses spread in a similar way.

In India, malaria cases have dropped sharply since 2000, but dengue outbreaks still fill hospitals in many cities after the [[monsoon|monsoon]]. In the USA, mosquitoes spread West Nile virus.

Mosquito [[larva|larvae]] live in water. Fish, tadpoles, dragonfly nymphs and water beetles eat them in huge numbers. Adult mosquitoes are snapped up by birds, [[@bats-fly|bats]], spiders, lizards and [[@frogs-monsoon|frogs]].

In the Arctic tundra, mosquitoes hatch in vast clouds each summer. Some scientists think migrating birds rely on them while raising chicks there. Others say mosquitoes make up only a small part of most animals' diets, and that midges and other flies could take their place.

The swarms can be so thick that herds of caribou change their routes across the tundra to escape them. Without mosquitoes, those great herds might walk different paths, trampling different plants.

People have tried many ways to control mosquitoes: draining swamps, spraying insecticides, using bed nets and putting fish in ponds. These help, but mosquitoes breed fast and some become resistant to sprays.

Scientists are now testing new methods. One uses a gene drive, a way of changing mosquitoes' [[@genes-family|genes]] so that a trait, such as producing only male babies, spreads quickly through a population. A project called Target Malaria is studying this for the mosquitoes that carry malaria in Africa. These ideas are being tested carefully before any large release.

Another method infects mosquitoes with a common bacterium called *Wolbachia*. It doesn't kill them, but it makes it much harder for them to pass on dengue. Cities in Indonesia, Brazil and Australia have seen big drops in dengue after releasing these mosquitoes.

Many scientists suggest a middle path. Out of about 3,500 mosquito species, only a few dozen spread serious human diseases. Targeting just those could save most of the lives while leaving the rest of nature mostly alone.

Some countries have already beaten malaria without wiping out mosquitoes. Sri Lanka, India's neighbour, was declared malaria-free by the WHO in 2016, through careful testing, treatment and mosquito control.

Mosquitoes are just one small group of insects. Remove all insects, though, and the effects would be far more dramatic, as the thought experiment in [[@what-if-no-insects|a world without insects]] shows.

text: In space there's no air or road to push against. So a rocket pushes on something it carries with it: its own exhaust. It throws hot gas out of the back at great speed, and the gas pushes the rocket forward.

Once a spacecraft is moving, it keeps going. Nothing in empty space slows it down. Earth's [[gravity|gravity]] is always pulling on it, though. Go fast enough sideways, and you keep falling around Earth instead of into it. That's an [[orbit|orbit]].

quiz.prompt: In empty space there is no air. So what pushes a rocket forward?

The gas it throws out backwards pushes it forwards
The Moon's gravity pulls it along

quiz.reveal: Every push has an equal push back. A rocket hurls hot gas out of its nozzle at enormous speed, and the gas shoves the rocket the other way. It works even better without air in the way.

sec.t:
More than 300 years ago, [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] described an experiment that couldn't be done. He imagined a cannon on top of a very tall mountain, above the air.

Fire the ball slowly and it falls to the ground nearby. Fire it faster and it lands farther away. Fire it fast enough and something odd happens. Earth's surface curves away beneath the ball as fast as the ball falls. It never lands. It just keeps falling, all the way around the world.

For a spacecraft just above the air, that speed is about 7.8 km a second. At that speed you could cross India from Kashmir to Kanyakumari in about seven minutes.

To change direction, a spacecraft fires small thrusters. Every push must be planned, because fuel is heavy and limited. Most of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel, burned in the first few minutes.

So engineers look for clever paths. India's [[@isro-missions|Mangalyaan]] circled Earth several times, firing its engine each time it swung close, to stretch its orbit before heading for Mars. Chandrayaan-3 did the same, looping around Earth and then around the Moon in carefully changed orbits before it landed. Spacecraft heading to the Moon or planets are aimed not at where their target is, but at where it will be when they arrive.

sec.h: A free push from a planet
sec.t:
Spacecraft can also borrow speed from planets. When a probe swoops close behind a moving planet, the planet's gravity flings it forward, a bit like a ball bouncing off the front of a moving train. This is called a gravity assist, or slingshot.

NASA's [[@voyager|Voyager probes]], launched in 1977, used Jupiter and Saturn this way. Voyager 2 also visited Uranus and Neptune. Both are now beyond the planets, more than 20 billion km away. They are still coasting at about 15 to 17 km a second, with no engine needed.

Not every engine has to roar. Some spacecraft use ion engines, which push out a thin stream of charged gas. The push is tiny, about the weight of a sheet of paper resting on your hand. But it can run for years. Little by little, the spacecraft speeds up until it is moving faster than a chemical [[@rockets-how|rocket]] alone could make it go.

text: Sunspots are dark patches on the surface of the Sun. They are not holes. They look dark because they are cooler than the rest of the surface: about 3,500 °C, compared with about 5,500 °C around them. They are still extremely hot and bright, just less bright than their surroundings.
They form where the Sun's magnetic field gets tangled into strong knots. Those knots stop hot gas from rising up from inside the Sun, so the area cools a little.
Sunspots come and go. Some last a few days, others for weeks. Their numbers rise and fall in a cycle of about 11 years. Many are larger than the whole Earth.

st.reveal: Sunspots march across the Sun's face and come back round again, showing that the Sun rotates. Galileo noticed this in the 1610s. Its middle spins faster than its poles, taking roughly 25 days at the equator.

sec.t:
For a long time, many people in Europe believed the heavens were perfect and unchanging. Yet sunspots had been seen long before telescopes. Chinese [[astronomer|astronomers]] recorded them more than 2,000 years ago, when haze or dust dimmed the Sun enough to glimpse large ones.

In the 1610s, several astronomers turned the new telescopes on the Sun. [[@galileo|Galileo]] studied sunspots carefully and argued that they were on the Sun itself and moved because the Sun was rotating. A spotty, spinning Sun did not fit old ideas about perfect heavens, which added to the arguments around his work.

Never try what they did. Looking at the Sun through a telescope or binoculars without a proper solar filter can blind you instantly.

{{story:galileo}}

In 1843, a German amateur astronomer named Heinrich Schwabe, who had counted sunspots for 17 years, noticed that their numbers rose and fell over about a decade. Later astronomers measured the cycle at about 11 years.

At solar minimum, the Sun can go weeks without a single spot. At solar maximum, there may be dozens at once. The busy years bring more solar flares and huge clouds of particles that can trigger [[@aurora|auroras]] and disturb satellites.

The current cycle, numbered 25, began in December 2019. In 2024, NASA and NOAA announced that the Sun had reached its maximum period. In May 2024, a giant sunspot group sent out storms that painted auroras across skies far from the poles. Astronomers at the Indian Astronomical Observatory in Hanle, [[@ladakh|Ladakh]], photographed a red glow on the horizon, a very rare sight in India.

sec.h: The quiet Sun and the cold winters
sec.t:
Between about 1645 and 1715, astronomers saw very few sunspots. This quiet stretch is called the Maunder Minimum, after the astronomers Annie and Walter Maunder, who studied the old records.

It overlapped with part of a chilly period known as the Little Ice Age, when rivers in Europe froze more often. Some scientists think the quiet Sun helped cool Earth. Others think volcanoes and natural changes in the oceans mattered more. Either way, the Little Ice Age was mild compared with the real [[@ice-ages|ice ages]], when giant ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe.

The Kodaikanal Solar Observatory, high in the Palani Hills of Tamil Nadu, has been photographing the Sun since the early 1900s. Its long record of sunspots is one of the longest in the world and is still used to study how the Sun changes over many cycles.

Today, spacecraft watch the Sun all day. NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory sends back images every few seconds, and India's [[@aditya-l1|Aditya-L1]], launched in 2023, watches the Sun without ever losing sight of it.

text: A lighthouse is a tower with a powerful light at the top that warns ships of danger and guides them safely to harbour. Lighthouses stand on rocky headlands, at the mouths of rivers and ports, and on lonely reefs far out at sea. At night, sailors look for their light. By day, they recognise each tower by its shape and painted stripes.

The light does not just shine. It flashes in a pattern called the lighthouse's character. One might flash white twice every ten seconds, another might show a long red flash. Sailors compare the pattern with their charts to know exactly which lighthouse they are seeing, and so where they are. The beam can often be seen 30 km or more away.

st.reveal: Every lighthouse has its own "character", such as two quick flashes every ten seconds. Sailors count the flashes and look them up on their charts. By day, the tower's paint pattern and shape do the same job.

sec.t:
A bare lamp spreads light in every direction, and most of it is wasted. Early lighthouses burned wood, coal or oil, and much of the glow disappeared into the sky. In 1822, a French scientist named Augustin-Jean Fresnel invented a new kind of lens. It was made of rings of [[@glass-made|glass]] [[prism|prisms]] arranged around the lamp like a beehive.

Each ring bends the light so that it all heads out in the same direction, in a strong, flat beam. A Fresnel lens is much thinner and lighter than an ordinary lens of the same power. Many lenses turned slowly on a bed of liquid mercury, so the beam swept round like a clock hand, giving a flash each time it passed. You can learn how lenses bend light in [[@lenses-glasses|lenses and glasses]].

India has nearly 200 lighthouses along its coasts and islands, looked after by the Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships. On the Marina in [[@chennai|Chennai]], a modern lighthouse lets visitors look out over one of the longest city beaches in the world. At [[@pallavas|Mahabalipuram]], an ancient rock temple on a hill is said to have been used as a beacon long ago, and a British lighthouse from the 1880s stands next to it.

Some lighthouses guard very remote places, such as tiny islands in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and [[@lakshadweep|Lakshadweep]]. In recent years, many Indian lighthouses have opened to visitors, with museums and viewing galleries.

For centuries, lighthouse keepers lived in or beside the towers. They trimmed wicks, polished lenses, wound up the clockwork that turned the light and sounded foghorns in bad weather. It was lonely work, especially on rocks far out at sea.

[[@electricity-history|Electric lamps]] replaced flames, and then the lights were automated. Today most lighthouses run on their own, often powered by [[@solar-panels|solar panels]], and are checked by visiting technicians. Ships now rely mainly on [[@gps-how|GPS]] and electronic charts. But a satellite signal can fail, and a light on a dark coast still means the same thing it did in ancient Alexandria: danger here, steer clear.

text: Yes. Whales live in and pass through the seas around India, though they are rarely seen from shore. Researchers have recorded around 30 kinds of whales and dolphins in Indian waters. Large whales seen here include the blue whale, the humpback, Bryde's whale and the sperm whale.

Blue whales, the largest animals that have ever lived, are seen off the coasts of Kerala, Maharashtra and Lakshadweep, and in big numbers off southern Sri Lanka. A rare group of humpback whales lives in the Arabian Sea all year round. Whales are protected by Indian law, and it is illegal to hunt them or trade in their parts.

sec.h: A whale cut off from the world
sec.t:
Most humpback whales spend summer feeding in cold polar waters, then swim thousands of kilometres to warm seas to breed. The Arabian Sea humpbacks don't. They stay in the warm waters off Oman, Pakistan and western India all year.

In 2014, scientists studying their DNA found that this group had been separated from other humpbacks for about 70,000 years. That may make it the most isolated whale population on Earth. Only a small number survive, probably fewer than 100. Fishermen and researchers have reported them off Gujarat, Maharashtra and Goa, and some have been [[@whale-songs|heard singing]] on underwater microphones.

Bryde's whales, pronounced "broo-dus", are among the most common large whales near India. They prefer warm water and eat small fish like sardines. Sperm whales, with their huge square heads, dive deep around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and off Sri Lanka, hunting squid in the dark.

Smaller toothed whales, such as pilot whales and false killer whales, also visit. Together with the river and coastal [[@dolphins-india|dolphins]], they make India an important place for whale research, even though many [[species|species]] are seldom seen.

Sometimes whales wash up on beaches, a stranding. In India, blue whales, Bryde's whales and pilot whales have stranded on beaches from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu. Scientists study each one to learn about the animal's life and what went wrong.

Whales face many dangers: getting tangled in fishing nets, being hit by ships, and noise from ships and seismic surveys that drowns out their calls. Plastic and chemical pollution add to the stress. In the past, whalers also prized ambergris, a waxy lump formed in sperm whales' guts and once prized for perfume. Selling it is now illegal in India, and police still seize smuggled lumps from time to time.

Spotting whales from India is still rare, but it is getting easier. Researchers place underwater microphones that record whale calls day and night, and fishermen share photos taken on phones. Some Indian coastal states have started tracking sightings so that scientists can map where whales go.

If you ever see a whale on a boat trip, stay calm and keep your distance. A blow of spray rising from the waves may be your only clue that a giant is passing just below.

text: Snake [[venom|venom]] is a mixture of [[protein|proteins]] made in special [[gland|glands]] in a snake's head. These glands are changed versions of the [[@gross-saliva|glands that make spit]]. When a venomous snake bites, [[@muscles|muscles]] squeeze the glands and push venom through hollow or grooved teeth called fangs, into the prey.

Different venoms attack different parts of the body. Some block the signals from nerves to muscles, so the prey can't move or breathe. Others stop blood from clotting, damage blood vessels or break down flesh. Many venoms do several of these things at once.
Snakes use venom mainly to catch and kill prey quickly, without a dangerous struggle. It also starts to digest the meal from the inside. Biting people is a last defence.

sec.t:
People often mix up the words, but they mean different things. Venom has to be injected, by a bite or a sting. Poison works when it is eaten, swallowed or touched. A cobra is venomous. A poison dart frog is poisonous.

Most snakes have no venom at all. Of nearly 4,000 kinds of snake, fewer than one in five are venomous, and only a few hundred are dangerous to people. India has over 300 kinds of snake, and most of them, like the rat snake that hunts mice in fields, are harmless.

Most serious snakebites in India come from four snakes, known as the Big Four. The spectacled cobra and the common krait have venom that mainly attacks nerves, causing weakness and trouble breathing. Russell's viper and the saw-scaled viper have venom that mainly stops blood from clotting.

Kraits hunt at night and sometimes slip into houses. Their bite can be almost painless, so a sleeping person may not notice. Sleeping on a raised bed under a tucked-in mosquito net helps keep them away.

A large study published in 2020 estimated that snakebites killed about 58,000 people a year in India between 2000 and 2019, mostly farm workers in villages. That is around half of all snakebite deaths in the world. In the USA, rattlesnakes and their relatives bite several thousand people a year, but only about five die, partly because hospitals with antivenom are usually close by.

{{story:immune-system}}

The only proven treatment for a serious snakebite is antivenom. To make it, horses are given tiny, safe doses of venom, slowly increased over weeks. Their [[@immune-system|immune system]] makes [[antibody|antibodies]] that grab hold of the venom. These antibodies are collected from the horses' blood and purified. The doses are kept small so the horses stay healthy.

Much of the venom comes from the Irula people near [[@chennai|Chennai]]. Their snake catchers' [[cooperative|cooperative]], started in 1978, catches snakes, gently collects their venom and releases them a few weeks later. The Irula are so skilled that in 2017, two of their snake catchers were invited to Florida to help track down invasive giant pythons.

Antivenom made for the Big Four doesn't work against every snake. Scientists in India are now working on antivenoms for other dangerous [[species|species]] too.

Venom is a toolbox of powerful chemicals, and scientists study it for new medicines. In the 1970s, researchers working with the venom of a Brazilian pit viper, which makes blood pressure drop, developed one of the first modern drugs for high blood pressure. Millions of people have taken medicines based on it.

Other venoms are being tested to make [[@blood|blood]] clot, to ease [[@pain|pain]] and to fight disease. A bite that can kill may one day help save lives. And if anyone is bitten, the best help is always calm, stillness and a fast trip to a [[@hospitals|hospital]].

text: The longest bridge on Earth is the Danyang–Kunshan Grand Bridge in China, 164.8 kilometres long. It opened in 2011 and carries the high-speed railway between Beijing and Shanghai. It's a viaduct, a long chain of short spans resting on pillars, crossing rice paddies, canals, rivers and a lake. A bullet train at full speed needs about half an hour to cross it.

Other bridges hold other records. The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana, USA, runs about 38 kilometres over water without a break. The Çanakkale 1915 Bridge in Turkey has the longest gap between two towers, 2,023 metres. In India, Mumbai's Atal Setu is the country's longest sea bridge, at about 21.8 kilometres.

sec.h: Why build a bridge over land?
sec.t:
China's [[@bullet-trains|bullet trains]] need tracks that are very flat and very straight. On the ground, that would mean flattening hills, filling hollows and cutting through villages and farms. Lifting the track onto pillars solves all of that. It also protects the line from floods and earthquakes, and leaves the fields underneath for farming.

Many of the world's longest bridges are railway viaducts in China, built this way in the 2000s and 2010s. Each section is made in a factory and lifted into place by huge machines, a bit like laying giant Lego bricks.

A suspension bridge hangs its road from thick steel cables draped over tall towers. It's the best design for crossing a wide gap without pillars in the middle. When San Francisco's [[@golden-gate|Golden Gate Bridge]] opened in 1937, its 1,280-metre main span was the longest in the world.

Today the record belongs to the Çanakkale 1915 Bridge over the Dardanelles strait in Turkey, opened in 2022. Its main span is 2,023 metres, about 20 football fields end to end. The number was chosen on purpose: 2023 was the 100th anniversary of the Turkish Republic.

Long bridges grow and shrink with the weather. Steel and concrete expand on hot days and contract on cold nights, so engineers leave gaps called expansion joints. When a car thumps over a metal strip on a bridge, it's usually crossing one of them.

Wind is a bigger danger for long suspension bridges. In 1940 a new bridge in Washington state, USA, nicknamed Galloping Gertie, began twisting in strong wind and tore itself apart only four months after it opened. Since then, engineers test models of big bridges in wind tunnels before building them.

In earthquake zones, bridges are designed to sway and slide a little without falling. While Japan's Akashi Kaikyō Bridge was being built, a huge earthquake in 1995 shifted its two towers, making the main span nearly a metre longer.

Atal Setu, opened in January 2024, links Mumbai to Navi Mumbai across the sea. It's nearly four times as long as the [[@india-wonder-bandra-sealink|Bandra–Worli Sea Link]]. Engineers had to protect flamingos in the mudflats below, so parts of the bridge carry noise barriers.

India also has one of the world's most dramatic bridges. The [[@india-wonder-chenab-bridge|Chenab Bridge]] in Jammu and Kashmir, opened to trains in 2025, carries a railway 359 metres above the river, higher than the Eiffel Tower. And the strangest part? Some of India's toughest bridges aren't built at all. In Meghalaya, people guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams until they become [[@india-wonder-living-root-bridges|living root bridges]].

text: Light bounces. When it hits a very smooth, shiny surface, it bounces off in a neat way. It leaves at the same angle it arrived, like [[@carrom|a carrom striker]] rebounding off the edge of the board. Because every ray keeps its pattern, the light coming off a mirror carries a clear picture.

Most surfaces, like paper or a wall, are rough when seen very close up. They scatter light in every direction, so you see the paper but not your face in it. A mirror is smooth all the way down to sizes far smaller than the waves of light. Modern mirrors are a sheet of [[@glass-made|glass]] with a very thin layer of silver or [[@aluminium|aluminium]] on the back, protected by paint. The glass keeps the metal flat and clean.

sec.t:
In the village of Aranmula in Kerala, a few families make a special metal mirror called the *Aranmula kannadi*. It is cast from a mix of metals whose exact recipe is a closely guarded secret, then polished for days by hand.

Because the shiny surface is on the front, with no glass on top, the reflection has no faint second image. Aranmula kannadi received a Geographical Indication tag, which means only mirrors made in that region may use the name. They are often given as gifts and are part of some Kerala wedding traditions.

The biggest [[@telescopes-how|telescopes]] use curved mirrors to collect starlight, because a large mirror is easier to build and support than a huge glass lens. The [[@hubble|Hubble]] Space Telescope's main mirror is 2.4 metres across. The [[@webb-telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]] has 18 gold-coated mirror segments. They unfolded in space to make one mirror 6.5 metres wide, about the length of two autorickshaws parked end to end. Gold reflects the [[infrared|infrared]] light Webb is built to see especially well.

In 1969, the crew of [[@apollo-moon|Apollo 11]] set up a panel of special mirrors on the Moon. Scientists on Earth fire lasers at it and time how long the light takes to return, about two and a half seconds. That's how they know the Moon is creeping away from us.

Most animals treat their reflection as a stranger, or ignore it. A few, such as chimpanzees, dolphins and magpies, seem to recognise themselves. In 2006, researchers at the Bronx Zoo in New York painted a white mark on the head of an Asian elephant named Happy. Looking into a giant mirror, she touched the mark with her trunk again and again, as if she knew the mark was on her own head.

That simple test hints at how clever [[@elephants-talk|elephants]] are. A mirror, after all, only bounces light. Knowing that the face in it is yours takes a brain.

text: Families come in many shapes. Some are a parent and a child. Some are two parents and their children. Some are large joint families with [[@pensions-old-age|grandparents]], uncles, aunts and cousins sharing one home. Some children are raised by [[@old-age-india|grandparents]], by one parent, by adoptive parents or by step-parents.

What families do is similar almost everywhere. They raise and protect children, share food and money, care for the sick and the old, and pass on language, stories, recipes and traditions. How they are arranged depends on history, culture, money, housing and personal choice.

myth: The "normal" family has always been a mother, a father and two children living on their own.

Small nuclear families became common in many countries only in the last century or so. For most of history, and in much of the world today, families often included grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins living close together or under one roof.

sec.t:
In a nuclear family, parents live with their children. In a joint family, common in India, several generations and the families of brothers often live together, sharing a kitchen and household costs. A grandmother might cook, a grandfather walk the children to school, and cousins grow up almost like brothers and sisters.

Indian households are getting smaller as people move to cities for work and live in apartments. Still, the average Indian household has between four and five people, compared with about two and a half in the United States. In Sweden and some other European countries, around four in ten households are just one person living alone.

In the United States, families living with several generations under one roof are becoming more common again. In 2021, about 18% of Americans lived in such homes, up from about 7% in 1971. High housing costs, care for older relatives and immigrant traditions all play a part. Many Indian-American families, for example, share their homes with grandparents.

Around the world, families are having fewer children. In 1950, women had about five children on average. Today the worldwide average is about 2.3. In India, it has fallen to about two, roughly the level at which a population stops growing in the long run. Better health care, more girls in school and the move to cities are major reasons. This changes the shape of the world's [[@population|population]].

Family words show how families work. [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] has separate words for your father's brother (*chacha*) and your mother's brother (*mama*), and for their wives. English uses "uncle" and "aunt" for all of them. Languages with many relative words often come from cultures where the wider family plays a large part in daily life.

Some people also talk about "chosen family", close friends who feel like relatives. In many Indian neighbourhoods, children call older neighbours aunty and uncle, and family-like ties stretch beyond blood.

Families also differ in how they celebrate, from multi-day [[@weddings-india|weddings]] to quiet dinners. Whatever shape a family takes, research suggests what matters most to children is feeling loved, safe and listened to. Your own [[@genes-family|genes]] come from your birth parents, but your family is the people who raise you.

text: A slum is a crowded neighbourhood where homes are often small and built from whatever is cheap. Many families there lack proper water, toilets and drains, or a legal right to their land.

Slums grow when people move to a city faster than it can provide homes they can afford. Newcomers usually come for work. Rent near jobs is high, and travelling in from far away costs money and hours. So people build or rent small rooms on any spare land close to work: beside railway lines, along rivers or on empty plots.

India's 2011 Census counted about 6.5 crore people living in slums, roughly one in every six people in its towns and cities. Around the world, UN-Habitat estimates that about one billion people live in slums or similar settlements.

sec.t:
When a city booms, jobs appear faster than housing. Building homes takes land, money and years of paperwork. A family arriving from a village, often through [[@migration-india|migration within India]], needs a roof the same week.

Land prices make things harder. In [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], squeezed onto a narrow [[peninsula|peninsula]], land is among the most expensive in India. Cheap rooms are hard to find anywhere near the trains and offices.

Many people living in slums have been there for decades. Their children go to school nearby, and they pay rent, run shops and vote. But without papers for their land, they can be moved out, and the city may refuse to lay water pipes or sewers there.

Slums are found far beyond India. In the late 1800s, New York's Lower East Side was packed with tenements: narrow buildings where [[@ellis-island|immigrant families]] from Europe crowded into dark rooms. In 1890, a [[@journalism|journalist]] named Jacob Riis published *How the Other Half Lives*, with photographs that shocked readers. It helped push the city to pass laws requiring windows, fresh air and toilets in new buildings.

Many of those same streets are now some of the most expensive in [[@new-york|New York]].

Cities have tried many things. Some knocked slums down and moved people to the edge of town, far from their jobs, and many families drifted back. Others have rebuilt homes on the same site, or given residents legal rights to their land so they could improve their own houses.

India's Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana, started in 2015, gives help to build or buy homes. Plans to redevelop Dharavi have been discussed for decades, and residents disagree about them. Some want new flats. Others worry about losing their workshops and neighbours. Most experts agree that the best plans are made with the people who live there, not just for them.

text: Village life in India is as varied as the country itself. [[@people-fishing-villages|A fishing village in Kerala]], a desert village in Rajasthan and a hill village in Nagaland look, sound and eat differently. But many share some things: farming, close-knit families, a weekly market, and neighbours who know each other's business.

About two in three Indians lived in villages at the 2011 [[@census|census]]. Most village households depend at least partly on farming, but people also work as weavers, potters, shopkeepers, teachers, drivers and builders. Many villages today have mobile phones, schools and paved roads that did not exist a generation ago.

sec.t:
Many villages wake before sunrise. Animals are fed and milked, water is fetched, and fires or gas stoves are lit for breakfast. Children walk or cycle to the village school, where a free hot lunch under the [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] scheme helps keep many of them in class.

Life often happens outdoors, on a shady platform under a big tree, at a place of worship or at the handpump. Then there is the weekly haat, a market where farmers sell vegetables and traders bring clothes, pots and bangles.

Villages elect a council called a [[@panchayat|panchayat]], headed by a sarpanch. It looks after roads, drains, water supply and local schemes. Since 1993, at least a third of panchayat seats must go to women, and many states reserve half.

For a long time, many villages had no [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. On 28 April 2018, the government announced that Leisang, a small village in Manipur, had been connected, the last inhabited village on its list. Not every home in every village had power yet, but the lines had reached all of them.

Since 2000, a national scheme has built lakhs of kilometres of rural roads, linking villages to towns, hospitals and markets. Mobile phones changed things too. Many village shopkeepers now take payments by scanning a QR code with [[@upi-payments|UPI]], and farmers check crop prices on their phones before deciding where to sell.

Villages are also places of strong traditions: [[@folk-music-india|folk songs]], local deities, crafts and stories handed down for centuries. Some have become famous for their own efforts. Mawlynnong in [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]] is known across India for its cleanliness, and Hiware Bazar in Maharashtra for collecting and [[@india-water-man|saving rainwater to beat drought]].

Village life also has real hardships. Incomes are often lower than in cities, good hospitals may be far away, and many young people leave to find work. Some come back during festivals, bringing city ideas home. Others return for good. For many Indians who live in cities, the family village is still the place they call home.

डॉक्टर इसे पैरेस्थीज़िया कहते हैं। यह तब होता है जब तुम कुछ देर तक किसी [[nerve|नस]] को दबाए रखते हो। नसें शरीर की तारें हैं, जो त्वचा और दिमाग के बीच संदेश ढोती हैं। एक नस को दबाओ, तो उसे खुराक देने वाली नन्ही [[capillary|केशिकाएँ]], यानी बाल जैसी पतली खून की नलियाँ, भी दब जाती हैं। ऑक्सीजन की कमी और दबाव से चपटी हुई नस आम संकेत भेजना बंद कर देती है, और पैर सुन्न हो जाता है।

sec.t:
तुम्हारा [[@nervous-system|तंत्रिका तंत्र]] लंबी-लंबी कोशिकाओं से बना है, जिन्हें [[neuron|न्यूरॉन]] कहते हैं। एक नस इनके हज़ारों पतले रेशों का गट्ठर है, जो किसी केबल के भीतर की तारों की तरह आपस में ठसाठस भरे होते हैं। सबसे तेज़ रेशे लगभग 120 मीटर प्रति सेकंड की रफ़्तार से संदेश ले जाते हैं। यह लगभग 430 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटा है, यानी पूरी रफ़्तार पर दौड़ती वंदे भारत एक्सप्रेस से भी दुगने से ज़्यादा।

रेशे अलग-अलग मोटाई के होते हैं। मोटे रेशे छूने का एहसास ढोते हैं, और यह भी कि तुम्हारा पैर कहाँ है। पतले रेशे दर्द और गर्माहट ढोते हैं। मोटे रेशों को ज़्यादा ऑक्सीजन चाहिए, इसलिए दबाव में वे सबसे पहले हार मान लेते हैं। इसीलिए सोते हुए पैर से सबसे पहले यह एहसास जाता है कि वह कहाँ रखा है, और खड़े होने पर तुम डगमगा जाते हो।

जब खून तेज़ी से वापस आता है, तो अलग-अलग रेशे थोड़े-थोड़े अलग समय पर फिर चालू होते हैं। दिमाग को आधे-अधूरे संदेशों की खिचड़ी मिलती है, और यही खिचड़ी झनझनाहट है।

पैर शरीर के ज़्यादातर हिस्सों से ज़्यादा बार इसलिए सोते हैं क्योंकि हम उसी ढंग से बैठते हैं। टाँग पर टाँग चढ़ाओ, तो ऊपर वाला घुटना नीचे वाले घुटने के ठीक नीचे, बाहर की तरफ़ की एक नस को दबा देता है। वहाँ यह नस त्वचा के बहुत पास होती है और उस पर गद्दी बहुत कम होती है।

पैरों के बल बैठने से टखने पर और पंजे के ऊपर की नसें दब जाती हैं। साइटिक नस, जो शरीर की सबसे मोटी नस है और लगभग तुम्हारे अँगूठे जितनी चौड़ी, कूल्हों से होकर हर टाँग के पीछे-पीछे नीचे जाती है। सख़्त फ़र्श पर लंबी स्कूल असेंबली, या लकड़ी की बेंच पर किसी धीमी पैसेंजर ट्रेन का लंबा सफ़र, इसे भी दबा सकते हैं।

बाँहों के साथ भी ऐसा होता है। बहुत-से लोग बाँह के ऊपर सो जाने के बाद सुन्न बाँह के साथ जागते हैं। और कोहनी की उस नस पर चोट लगे, जिसे अंग्रेज़ी में [[@body-funny-bone|‘फ़नी बोन’]] कहते हैं, तो पल भर में झनझनाहट का झटका लगता है।

सुन्नपन बेकार लगता है, पर चुभन एक चेतावनी है। यह तुम्हें हिलने पर मजबूर करती है, इससे पहले कि दबाव कोई असली नुकसान करे। घंटों दबी रहने वाली त्वचा और नसें खराब हो सकती हैं। इसीलिए जो मरीज़ खुद करवट नहीं ले सकते, नर्सें उनकी करवट बदलती रहती हैं, अक्सर लगभग हर दो घंटे पर, ताकि दर्दनाक घाव न बनें।

सबसे तेज़ इलाज आसान है। बैठने का ढंग बदलो, पैर की उँगलियाँ हिलाओ, और एक मिनट रुको। पर खड़े धीरे से होना। सुन्न पैर दिमाग को बता नहीं पाता कि वह कैसे रखा है, इसलिए पहले ही कदम पर टखना मुड़ जाना आसान है।

अटपटे ढंग से बैठने के बाद की झुनझुनी आम और बेनुकसान है। पर अगर झनझनाहट बिना किसी दबाव के हो, बहुत देर तक रहे या बार-बार लौटे, तो बात अलग है। किसी भरोसेमंद बड़े या डॉक्टर को बताना ठीक है। बड़ों में यह कभी-कभी कुछ खास [[@vitamins|विटामिनों]] की कमी से, जैसे बी12, या नसों पर असर डालने वाली बीमारियों से जुड़ा हो सकता है।

और सोते हुए पैर की सबसे अजीब बात? कुछ मिनटों के लिए वह तुम्हें एक ऐसी इंद्रिय दिखा देता है जिसे तुम दिन भर बिना ध्यान दिए इस्तेमाल करते हो: बिना देखे यह जानना कि तुम्हारा शरीर कहाँ है। वैज्ञानिक इसे [[@senses-more|मशहूर पाँच इंद्रियों से आगे की इंद्रियों]] में गिनते हैं।

text: The Dust Bowl was a disaster on the Great Plains of the USA during the 1930s. A long [[drought|drought]] dried out farmland that had been ploughed up only a few years earlier. Strong winds then lifted the loose topsoil into giant dust storms called "black blizzards".

Some storms were so thick that people could not see their own hands. Crops died, animals choked and many families lost their farms. About 2.5 million people left the Plains states by 1940. The disaster changed how the USA, and later the world, thinks about protecting soil.

sec.t:
For thousands of years, the southern plains were covered in tough prairie grass. Its deep roots held the soil in place through droughts and storms, and fed huge herds of bison. Native American nations hunted there long before settlers came.

From the late 1800s, settlers arrived with ploughs. During the First World War, wheat prices soared, and tractors made it easy to plough faster than ever. Millions of acres of grass were ripped up and replaced with wheat. When prices crashed and rain stopped in the early 1930s, fields were left bare. The roots that had held the soil for centuries were gone.

In May 1934, one huge storm blew dust over 2,000 km east. It fell on Chicago, New York and Washington, DC, and settled on ships far out in the Atlantic. Suddenly, people in big eastern cities could see the problem for themselves.

A soil scientist named Hugh Hammond Bennett had been warning about soil loss for years. In 1935, as he spoke to members of Congress in Washington, another dust cloud from the plains darkened the sky outside. Soon afterwards, Congress created the Soil Conservation Service to help farmers protect their land.

The Dust Bowl hit at the same time as the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]], when banks failed and jobs disappeared. Many families packed everything into old cars and drove west along [[@route-66|Route 66]] towards California, hoping for farm work. They were often called "Okies", even if they were not from Oklahoma, and many were treated badly when they arrived.

The writer John Steinbeck told their story in his 1939 novel *The Grapes of Wrath*. Singer Woody Guthrie wrote songs about the dust and the long road west. Photographers hired by the government took pictures that are still in museums today.

Slowly, things improved. The government paid farmers to plant grass, plough along the curves of hills and rotate crops. Workers planted about 220 million trees in long shelterbelts from the Canadian border down to Texas to break the wind. The rains returned around 1939. The lesson that [[@soil-made|soil]] takes centuries to make and only days to lose still guides farming everywhere. India met the same question during its own push to grow more food, the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]]: how to farm hard without wearing the land out.

text: Paris has been called the City of Light, or *la Ville Lumière*, for two reasons. In the 1660s, the city's police chief ordered lanterns to be hung in the streets, making Paris one of the first big cities lit at night. Later came gas lamps and then electric lights.

In the 1700s, Paris was also a centre of the Enlightenment, a time when thinkers argued for science, reason and [[@human-rights|human rights]]. The "light" can mean ideas as well as lamps. Today Paris is the capital of France and one of the most visited cities in the world.

sec.h: From an island to a capital
sec.t:
More than 2,000 years ago, a tribe called the Parisii lived on an island in the River Seine. The Romans conquered them and built a town called Lutetia. The island, now the Île de la Cité, is still the heart of Paris.

On it stands Notre-Dame, a [[@gothic-cathedrals|Gothic cathedral]] begun in 1163. In April 2019, a fire destroyed its roof and spire. Craftspeople spent five years rebuilding them, using oak beams and traditional tools, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

In 1889, France held a giant world fair to mark 100 years since the [[@french-revolution|French Revolution]]. The engineer Gustave Eiffel's company built an iron tower about 300 m tall as its entrance. It was the tallest structure in the world until 1930.

Many artists hated it. It was supposed to come down after 20 years, but scientists used it for radio experiments, and the army found it useful for sending signals. So it stayed. Now with its antennas it is about 330 m tall, and the [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] is repainted by hand about every seven years.

The [[@famous-paintings|Louvre]] was once a royal palace. It opened as a public museum in 1793 and is now the most visited museum in the world. Its most famous painting, the [[@mona-lisa|Mona Lisa]] by [[@leonardo|Leonardo da Vinci]], hangs behind thick glass.

In the late 1800s, painters such as [[@impressionists-monet|Claude Monet]] worked in and around Paris, painting outdoors and catching changing light. Their style, called [[@impressionism|Impressionism]], changed art. Many of their works hang in the Musée d'Orsay, a museum in an old railway station.

In the 1850s and 1860s, the city's planner Baron Haussmann knocked down many crowded [[medieval|medieval]] streets and built wide avenues called boulevards. They were lined with trees and cream-coloured stone buildings of the same height. Much of Paris still looks this way. The Métro, the [[@metro-trains|underground railway]], opened in 1900, and its old station entrances have curving green ironwork.

sec.h: A city of cafés and bread
sec.t: Paris is famous for its cafés, where people sit at small round tables on the pavement, watching the street. Many Parisians buy a fresh baguette, a long thin loaf, every day. Bakers compete each year for the prize of best baguette in Paris, and the winner supplies bread to the French president's palace for a year.

text: Nobody invented peanut butter all at once. People in South and Central America, including the Aztecs, were grinding roasted peanuts into paste centuries ago. In 1884, a Canadian named Marcellus Gilmore Edson took out a [[@patents|patent]] on a peanut paste made by grinding roasted peanuts between heated surfaces.

In the 1890s, the American doctor John Harvey [[@cereal-history|Kellogg]] made nut butters for patients at his health resort. Soon after, inventors built machines to grind peanuts in large amounts. Peanut butter was sold to crowds at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis, and it never looked back. The scientist George Washington Carver is often named as its inventor, but he was not.

sec.t:
Peanuts are not really nuts. They are [[legume|legumes]], relatives of peas, beans and the many kinds of [[@pulses-dal|dal]] eaten in India. The plant is a low, leafy bush with small yellow flowers.

After a flower is [[@pollinators|pollinated]], something odd happens. Its stalk grows longer, bends downwards and pushes the young pod into the soil. The peanuts grow underground, which is why they are also called groundnuts. Farmers dig the whole plant up to harvest them.

sec.h: From the Andes to the world

sec.t:
George Washington Carver was born into slavery in Missouri in the 1860s and became a scientist and teacher at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama. Cotton farming had worn out the soil of the American South. Carver urged farmers to also grow peanuts and other legumes, which put nitrogen back into the [[@soil-made|soil]].

To give farmers a market for their crop, he searched for new uses. He developed or popularised hundreds of peanut products and recipes, from dyes to milk substitutes. He became so famous for peanuts that people assumed he must have invented peanut butter too. In 1921 he even spoke to a committee of the [[@congress-usa|US Congress]] about the many uses of the peanut.

Early peanut butter had a problem: the oil separated and floated to the top, and it could go rancid. In the 1920s, a businessman named Joseph Rosefield found a way to keep the oil mixed in by adding a small amount of hardened oil. This made the smooth, creamy jars sold in American supermarkets. Today's "natural" peanut butters skip the hardened oil, which is why you have to stir them before spreading.

Peanut butter and jelly [[@food-sandwich-name|sandwiches]] became an American [[@lunch-world|school-lunch classic]]. During the Second World War, American soldiers carried peanut butter in their rations. In India, peanut butter has become far more common in recent years, and many jars on the shelves are made from Indian groundnuts.

For most people peanuts are a cheap, healthy source of [[protein|protein]]. But for some, even a tiny amount can cause a serious allergic reaction. That is why many schools in the United States, and some in India, have strict rules about peanuts. If a friend has a [[@food-allergies|food allergy]], never share food without checking with an adult first.
